- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant stated that illuminated manuscripts were created using parchment, vellum, or paper for the pages, and ink, pigments made from plants and minerals, and gold or silver leaf for decoration.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant provided historical context explaining that illuminated manuscripts were luxury items for wealthy patrons, such as monasteries, nobles, and the church, and that the use of gold and silver leaf was to enhance artistic beauty and convey the spiritual importance of the text.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant explained that illuminated manuscripts were labor-intensive and produced during a time when the production and distribution of books were limited by high costs, lack of printing presses, and low literacy rates.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant noted that illuminated manuscripts were commissioned by wealthy patrons who viewed them as valuable symbols of status and commissioned them to glorify religious texts, preserve literary works, or commemorate important events.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant emphasized that the idea of mass production of books for the general public was not a reality during the medieval and Renaissance periods, and that the use of costly materials was seen as appropriate for commemorating texts and preserving them for future generations.
